claims.text: The initial AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles are smaller than 5 nm.
The PLD-grown AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles initially have an FCC crystal structure.
The initial nanoparticles exhibit elliptical or icosahedral morphology on a silicon nitride membrane.
A surface-energy gradient drives Au and Cu atoms to migrate rapidly to nanoparticle surfaces during heating.
Au and Cu have lower surface energies than Co, Ni, and Pt.
Segregation produces an Au/Cu-rich shell and a Co/Ni/Pt-rich core.
The Au/Cu-enriched surface layer subsequently evaporates.
Configurational-entropy stabilization is insufficient to counteract surface-energy minimization in sub-10 nm AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles.
Heating overcomes the activation barrier for surface diffusion of Au and Cu.
Evaporation-driven composition changes lower the nanoparticle melting point.
Evaporation-driven composition changes accelerate nanoparticle coalescence.
The apparent sluggish diffusion is a kinetic artifact of the initial nanoparticle state rather than a persistent barrier to surface reconstruction.
The dominant segregation and evaporation mechanism begins at approximately 850 K, with an uncertainty of ±50 K.
Above the critical temperature, the rate of Au/Cu surface segregation exceeds the rate of bulk diffusion.
Crossing the critical temperature causes a sharp increase in the evaporation rate of surface atoms.
Crossing the critical temperature causes a rapid elliptical-to-spherical shape transition.
Surface-species evaporation decreases average particle size through mass loss.
Surface-energy minimization alone can drive the segregation without overcoming bulk-diffusion barriers.
The proposed mechanism applies primarily to particles below 10 nm and is expected to fail above 20 nm, where bulk entropy dominates.
Icosahedral particles segregate faster than truncated-octahedral particles because they have greater surface strain and a different segregation activation energy.
